entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Old-fashioned cheer - now often used ironically.

entries.definition: (of a female body) healthily plump and vigorous
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Dated approval of a full, healthy figure - warmth with an old-fashioned air.
examples: a generation ago … buxom actresses were popular

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The archaic-sounding form, and used now only when the writer wants that flavour.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Like enraged, but it keeps the cause in view: something did this to them.
examples: infuriated onlookers charged the police who were beating the boy

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The plain word, and a loaded one: neutral of a cut of meat, personal and often wounding of a person.
examples: he hadn't remembered how fat she was

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Willing to try - courage as good sportsmanship rather than heroism.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Force without proportion - more was applied than the thing needed.
examples: incensed at the government's heavy-handed economic policies

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Quick to learn - formal and slightly old-fashioned.

entries.definition: having an abundant supply of money or possessions of value
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Blunt and slightly envious - conspicuously rich.

entries.definition: having an abundant supply of money or possessions of value
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Substantial and settled money - more dignified than 'rich'.

entries.label: neutral
entries.tone: Noise as a good time - *a rip-roaring success* has no complaint in it at all.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Warm in form rather than in feeling - a cordial greeting can be perfectly correct and quite cold.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Cowardice joined to malice; now often played for comedy.
examples: the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on … December 7th

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The plain word - direct, and heavy enough that lawyers prefer 'take'.
examples: Someone stole my wallet on the train
This author stole entire paragraphs from my dissertation

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The adverb of *dandy*: old-fashioned cheer - now often used ironically.
examples: she had shown her talents dandily

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The adverb of *buoyant*: cheer that resists being pushed down; the metaphor is a thing that will not sink.

entries.definition: showing or motivated by sympathy and understanding and generosity
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Capacity, not just intent: there is room in this person for more than their own concerns.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Praises ease of manner in someone who need not have bothered - it fits people with standing.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Homely and old, and the craft is entirely in the deceiving.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The adverb of *sage*: wisdom that came with age, and the noun stands just behind the adjective.

entries.definition: showing a lack of judgment or experience
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Names the mechanism: this person believes things on insufficient evidence.
examples: so credulous he believes everything he reads

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The hand that will not open; the oldest image in the family.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The everyday word for full anger - vivid, and still sympathetic to whoever feels it.

entries.definition: express complaints, discontent, displeasure, or unhappiness
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: From Yiddish, and affectionate as often as not - the complaining is a known habit.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Carries the weight of proof - used where provenance has actually been checked.

entries.definition: in an unfortunate or deplorable manner
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The adverb of *deplorable*: formal censure, expecting the reader to share the judgement.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Price used as a verdict on quality, which is the oldest trick in the word.
examples: a cheap plastic toy that broke in a day

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Praise for a child, and a hint of too many questions for an adult.
examples: if someone saw a man climbing a light post they might get inquisitive

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The adverb of *contented*: settled rather than delighted; it describes a steady state, not a mood.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Respectful and gentle - names the death while keeping the person in view.

entries.definition: very thin especially from disease or hunger or cold
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Clinical and grave - thinness as the visible mark of illness or starvation.
examples: The rescued dogs were emaciated and barely able to stand.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The adverb of *perky*: brisk and a little relentless - it can condescend when said of an adult.
examples: stuck perkily, like a bustle on a woman's skirt

entries.definition: distorted and unnatural in shape or size; abnormal and hideous
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Ugliness that frightens; also used of moral wrong.

entries.definition: find fault with; express criticism of; point out real or perceived flaws
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The neutral verb - it names the act without saying whether it was deserved.
examples: The paper criticized the new movie

entries.label: neutral
entries.tone: *Dying to know* - hyperbole worn so smooth the death has gone out of it.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Technical and rare, from the same root as *attrition*.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Blames the absence of a method rather than the absence of effort.
examples: a most haphazard system of record keeping

entries.definition: slow to learn or understand; lacking intellectual acuity
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Gently disparaging, common in British use.
examples: never met anyone quite so dim

entries.definition: feeling self-respect or pleasure in something by which you measure your self-worth; or being a reason for pride
entries.label: neutral
entries.tone: Genuinely two-faced: proud of your children is warm, proud to a fault is a failing. Context decides.

entries.definition: absorbed in your own interests or thoughts etc
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Inattentive rather than grasping; the harm is what gets overlooked.

entries.definition: in a slim or slender manner
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The adverb of *slender*: admiring - thinness with grace built into the word.

entries.definition: being of delicate or slender build
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: High praise with a touch of glamour - slim, elegant and stylish at once.
examples: svelte in a black evening dress

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Cheapness with a whiff of the shabby-genteel about it.

entries.definition: marked by deliberate deceptiveness especially by pretending one set of feelings and acting under the influence of another
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Blunt and personal - the accusation you make to someone's face, or behind their back.

entries.definition: marked by deliberate deceptiveness especially by pretending one set of feelings and acting under the influence of another
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The coldest word in the family; it implies a practised double life rather than a single deception.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Soft and everyday - what people say when 'dead' is too hard to say.
examples: She's been gone three years now.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The plain, warm verb - no judgement attached.

entries.definition: hasty and without attention to detail; not thorough
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The work was done to be seen to be done; it accuses the motive, not the skill.
